title: Yassa Yapp
author: Aïssatou Mbaye
desc: A leg of lamb done as a méchoui in the pot — the stuffing divided in three, two hours on low heat, done when the leg is tender and nearly all the water has evaporated.
longDesc: Her lamb yassa, and her own framing is that it is a méchoui done in a pot rather than over a fire. The stuffing is pounded garlic, pepper, salt, half a bell pepper and bird's eye chillies, divided in three. The leg is stuffed through incisions, one portion of the stuffing spread on it with two tablespoons of mustard and the juice of a lemon. Half a diced onion and the other half-pepper brown in oil, the lamb goes in with a full glass of water, and it simmers covered on low heat for two hours. The sauce takes the last third of the stuffing with the juice of a large lemon and, optionally, some of the braising liquid, finished with mustard near the end.
ingredients: // Quantities printed only inside the method
Leg of lamb — gigot, quantity not printed
The juice of 1 lemon, for the lamb
The juice of 1 large lemon, for the sauce
A little water, a little oil
equipment: Heavy pot with a lid — marmite
steps: Pound the garlic, pepper, salt, half the bell pepper and the bird's eye chillies into a stuffing, and divide it in three.
Stuff the leg of lamb through incisions.
Spread one portion of the stuffing over the lamb with 2 tablespoons of mustard and the juice of one lemon.
Brown half the diced onion and the other half of the pepper in oil, until the onion is well browned.
Add the lamb and a well-filled glass of water, cover, and leave it to simmer on low heat for 2 hours.
Watch the cooking closely. It is done when the leg is tender and nearly all the water has evaporated.
Soften the onions in hot oil with a bay leaf and a chilli.
Once the onions turn translucent, add the remaining stuffing, salt, pepper and the juice of a large lemon.
Add a little water, and some of the lamb braising juices if you like.
Simmer a few minutes and add the mustard near the end. The sauce must have a good golden colour.
chefTips: Tender, and nearly all the water evaporated — two conditions, and both have to be true. That is the clearest braising endpoint in the Senegalese material.
Divide the stuffing in three. One third into the incisions, one third spread on the outside with the mustard and lemon, one third into the sauce.
A well-filled glass of water for a two-hour braise is very little liquid, and that is the point — it is a méchoui in a pot, not a stew.
Watch it closely is her own instruction, and with that little water it is not optional.
Mustard near the end of the sauce, not at the start. Same rule as her other yassas.
Your sauce must have a good golden colour — the second cue, for the sauce rather than the meat.
Her own note: lamb yassa is as good as chicken yassa and nobody thinks of it, especially for people who like meat. She is right, and the two-hour braise is why.
commonMistakes: Adding more water, which turns it into a stew.
Stuffing the lamb without also spreading stuffing on the outside.
Leaving it unattended through the two hours.
Pulling it when tender but still wet.
sources: Adapted from 'Yassa Yapp', aistoucuisine.com, path /publications/yassa-agneau. BYLINE: Aïssatou Mbaye. Date as printed: 20 mai 2016; page metadata records a modified date of 2024-06-15, A DATE DISCREPANCY flagged as seen. Yield: NONE PRINTED. TWO-PASS on all step figures. 'Yapp' in the title is Wolof for meat, though the page does not label it as Wolof.

A STRUCTURAL ABSENCE: NO INGREDIENT LIST REACHES THE PAGE'S HTML. Quantities exist only inside the steps, and only these, confirmed by both passes: '2 cas de moutarde'; 'un verre d'eau bien rempli'; 'la moitié d'un oignon'; 'la moitié du poivron'; 'l'autre tiers de la farce'; 'le jus d'un citron' and 'le jus d'un gros citron'; 'une feuille de laurier'; 'un peu d'eau' and 'un peu d'huile'. NAMED WITHOUT QUANTITY: gousses d'ail, poivre, sel, piments oiseau, oignons, and the gigot itself. The six servings above is editorial and no lamb weight has been invented.

DONENESS CUES as printed in French, and this entry is unusually rich in them: 'Lorsque l'oignon est bien doré' — when the onion is well browned; 'lorsque l'huile est un peu chaude' — when the oil is somewhat hot; 'lorsque les oignons deviennent translucides' — when the onions turn translucent; 'Bien surveiller la cuisson' — watch the cooking closely; 'le gigot est tendre et presque tout l'eau est évaporée' — the leg is tender and nearly all the water has evaporated; and 'Votre sauce doit avoir une belle couleur doré' — your sauce must have a good golden colour.
NO NUMERIC TEMPERATURE appears anywhere — the only heat instruction is 'feu doux', low heat. The one explicit time is 'laisser mijoter à feu doux pendant 2h'.

CULTURAL REMARKS as printed: 'On y pense pas souvent mais le Yassa à l'agneau est aussi bon que le Yassa au poulet surtout pour les amateurs de viande' — nobody often thinks of it, but lamb yassa is as good as chicken yassa, especially for meat lovers. And her method framing: 'Pour cette recette je propose de faire un méchoui à la marmite' — for this recipe I suggest doing a méchoui in the pot.

A RETRIEVAL NOTE: the site is JavaScript-rendered and its ingredient lists were systematically unreachable. The figures above came from a structured data-extraction pass rather than verbatim transcription.
reheating: Gentle covered heat with a splash of water.
healthBenefits: Lamb is high in protein, iron, zinc and vitamin B12.
A long low braise with very little liquid retains the meat's own juices.
Lemon juice at this quantity supplies vitamin C.
culturalNote: Méchoui is the whole roast lamb of North and West African feasts, and a cook proposing to do one in a pot on a Thursday is exactly how a festival dish becomes a family one. The two-hour braise in barely a glass of water is the closest a kitchen gets to a fire.
